claims.text: The WTaTiVZr alloy is equimolar, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each constituent element.
Commercially used pure tungsten has a conventional BCC lattice.
Chemical complexity in equimolar WTaTiVZr produces severe atomic-scale local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr hinder vacancy-mediated dislocation climb.
Local lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr hinder grain-boundary diffusion.
Retarded vacancy diffusion and suppressed dislocation climb increase the alloy's activation energy for creep.
Suppression of diffusion-controlled deformation delays dislocation motion and crack initiation.
Delayed dislocation motion and crack initiation improve the plastic-strain capacity and toughness of WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten.
The proposed diffusion and climb mechanism is responsible for enhanced high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten.
At 1200–1500 °C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit significantly less creep displacement than pure tungsten under matched test conditions.
At 1200–1500 °C, WTaTiVZr will have a higher measured creep activation energy than pure tungsten.
At 1200–1500 °C, WTaTiVZr will have a lower activation volume than pure tungsten.
Agreement between nanoindentation and macroscopic creep measurements would support diffusion-controlled mechanism suppression as the dominant factor.
Pure tungsten has lower creep activation energies than equimolar WTaTiVZr.
High-temperature creep in pure tungsten is conventionally dominated by vacancy diffusion.
The proposed mechanism applies in the 1200–1500 °C range under inert atmospheres.
Lower temperatures or non-inert environments may activate different deformation mechanisms.
Nanoindentation creep results may not quantitatively scale to bulk deformation behavior.
A lack of statistically significant differences in activation energy, activation volume, and creep displacement between the alloy and pure tungsten would falsify the proposed mechanism.
